content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe different methods for separating mixtures
Choose appropriate separation methods based on the properties of components
Explain the principles behind each separation technique
Describe practical procedures for common separations
Mixtures can be separated into their individual components using
. The method chosen depends on the physical properties of the substances in the mixture. No chemical reactions occur during separation.
An insoluble solid from a liquid
The liquid passes through small holes in the filter paper, but the solid particles are too large to pass through.
Fold filter paper and place in funnel
Pour mixture into the filter paper
A dissolved solid (solute) from a solution
The solvent evaporates, leaving the solid behind.
This method may decompose heat-sensitive substances.
A dissolved solid from a solution (gives pure crystals)
A hot saturated solution is cooled slowly, allowing pure crystals to form.
Heat the solution to evaporate some solvent
Test by dipping a cold glass rod - crystals should form on it
Produces purer, larger crystals without decomposition.
A liquid from a solution (recovers the solvent)
The liquid is evaporated and then condensed back to liquid form.
Heat the solution in the flask
Solvent evaporates and rises as vapour
Vapour passes into condenser where cold water cools it
Obtaining pure water from salt water
Miscible liquids with different boiling points
Liquids evaporate at different temperatures. A fractionating column provides surfaces for liquids to condense and re-evaporate, improving separation.
Plus fractionating column (filled with glass beads)
Liquid with lowest boiling point evaporates first
Temperature rises, next liquid evaporates and is collected
Different substances have different solubilities, so they travel at different speeds through the stationary phase.
Draw a pencil line near the bottom of the paper (not pen!)
Place a small spot of mixture on the line
Lower paper into solvent (solvent below the pencil line)
Allow solvent to rise up the paper
Remove when solvent nearly reaches the top
Mark the solvent front and dry
$$R_f = \frac{\text{Distance travelled by substance}}{\text{Distance travelled by solvent}}$$
The denser liquid sinks and can be drained off.
Open tap to drain lower layer
Close tap when lower layer has drained
Using evaporation to get pure water from salt water
Use distillation to recover the water; evaporation leaves salt behind
Using a pen to draw the line in chromatography
Use pencil - pen ink would dissolve and affect results
Having the solvent level above the spot in chromatography
The spot must be above the solvent level
Name the method you would use to separate:
a) Sand from salt water (1 mark) b) Pure water from ink (1 mark) c) Food dyes in a sweet (1 mark)
Describe how you would obtain pure, dry crystals of copper sulfate from copper sulfate solution. (4 marks)
Explain why fractional distillation is used instead of simple distillation to separate ethanol and water. (3 marks)
In a chromatography experiment, a substance travels 4.2 cm and the solvent travels 6.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value. (2 marks)
A student wants to obtain pure salt from rock salt (a mixture of salt and sand). Describe the steps they should take. (5 marks)
Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper
Removing a solvent by heating to leave a solid behind
Obtaining pure crystals by cooling a saturated solution
Separating a liquid from a solution by evaporation and condensation
Separating liquids with different boiling points using a fractionating column
Separating dissolved substances based on their movement through a medium
Ratio of distance travelled by substance to distance travelled by solvent
The solid left on the filter paper
The liquid that passes through the filter paper
Mixtures are separated by physical methods based on properties
